text: Query-based (polling) CDC needs a column like LAST_UPDATE_TIMESTAMP on every table. It cannot see rows deleted since the last poll and misses intermediate updates between polls. Log-based CDC captures all of these.
why: Shows the concrete cost of the row-by-row method.

text: MongoDB does expose its changes: Debezium's MongoDB connector delegates oplog capture to MongoDB change streams. This needs a replica set or sharded cluster. A standalone server has no oplog, but a one-member replica set works.
why: Corrects the MongoDB example and gives the requirement.

text: A PostgreSQL replication slot keeps all WAL its consumer still needs, even while the CDC tool is down. That is how it can resume, but an abandoned slot can fill pg_wal. max_slot_wal_keep_size caps this, and unused slots should be dropped.
why: Resuming after an outage has a disk-space cost on Postgres.

text: MySQL purges binlogs after a retention period. If a Debezium connector restarts after its position was purged, it fails with an error that a new snapshot is needed; snapshot.mode=when_needed makes it re-snapshot automatically.
why: Resume is not unconditional on MySQL.

text: Logs do not hold the full history, so CDC tools start with an initial snapshot (a full SELECT of each table) and then stream changes from the log position recorded at that point. Debezium does this on first start, and so does Airbyte's first CDC sync.
why: Explains how existing rows get to the sink.

text: The outbox pattern combines the two approaches. The service writes an event row to an 'outbox' table in the same transaction as its business data, and CDC (e.g. Debezium) tails the log and publishes those rows to Kafka. You get application-context events without the dual-write risk.
why: The standard way to get app-context events reliably via CDC.

text: PostgreSQL 15 and earlier allow logical replication slots only on the primary. From PostgreSQL 16 a slot can be created on a standby (set hot_standby_feedback), and PostgreSQL 17 adds failover-enabled slots so Debezium can continue after promotion.
why: Version condition for 'run CDC on a replica' on Postgres.

text: On MySQL, a replica writes changes it receives from its source into its own binlog only when log_replica_updates is enabled. It is enabled by default in MySQL 8.4 unless binary logging is turned off, and CDC needs it to read from that replica.
why: Configuration condition for MySQL replica-based CDC.

text: Checkpointing prevents loss but not duplicates. Debezium says that after a crash consumers see every event 'at least once', and PostgreSQL may resend recent changes after a server crash. Sinks should apply changes idempotently, e.g. upsert by primary key.
why: Learners should design sinks for at-least-once delivery.

text: CDC emits one event per changed row, not per transaction. Debezium can add BEGIN/END transaction boundary events and transaction IDs if provide.transaction.metadata is set to true (default false). Consumers can use these to regroup a transaction.
why: How to keep transaction grouping downstream.

text: Airbyte does not treat CDC sources as infinite streams. Each scheduled sync reads from the last saved log position, so replication lag is at least the sync interval, and syncs must run often enough to read the logs before they are purged.
why: Sets expectations for lag with Airbyte versus streaming tools like Debezium.

text: In PostgreSQL 'only one receiver may consume changes from a slot at any given time'; each independent consumer needs its own slot. Debezium's PostgreSQL connector 'always uses a single task'.
why: Explains why one log stream has one active reader.

text: Redshift's built-in way to export to S3 is UNLOAD, which writes query results as text, CSV, JSON or Parquet files. By default it writes in parallel, one or more files per slice.
why: Gives the native alternative the teacher alluded to.

text: MySQL caches a transaction's changes until COMMIT and then writes the entire transaction to the binary log before the commit completes, so the binlog is in commit order. The binlog is a replication/recovery log, separate from InnoDB's redo log.
why: Clarifies which MySQL log CDC actually reads.

text: Airbyte CDC limits: most sources support CDC only on tables with a primary key, views are not supported, and only INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE are captured (TRUNCATE and ALTER do not appear). New tables need a snapshot before CDC tracks them.
why: Practical gotchas for the suggested homework.

text: With Debezium on Kafka Connect, fan-out is cheap: the source is read once into Kafka topics, and separate sink connectors stream those topics to Elasticsearch, a warehouse, and so on. An Airbyte connection links one source to one destination.
why: Shows how fan-out works in each tool.
